notes: difficulty is derived from the Bloom level: Remember and Understand are easy, Apply is medium, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create are hard.

questions.question_text: Which statement best defines an open educational resource (OER)?

options.A: Any educational resource that the user can read or download without paying
options.B: Any complete textbook that a university makes available to read online
options.C: Any educational resource that has passed a peer review by its publisher
options.D: An educational resource that is in the public domain or carries an open license

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. An OER is an educational resource that is in the public domain or carries an open license, so anyone may use, adapt, and share it without asking first. Option A describes a free resource, which may still forbid copying and editing. Options B and C describe a source and a quality check, and the definition requires neither. Openness is about permission, not about price, publisher, or approval.

questions.question_text: Under U.S. law, when does copyright protection for a new work begin?

options.A: When the creator registers the work with the Copyright Office
options.B: Automatically, when the work is fixed in a tangible form such as a saved file
options.C: When the creator adds a © symbol and an "all rights reserved" notice
options.D: When the creator publishes the work for sale or posts it online

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Protection begins the moment a work is fixed in a tangible form, such as a typed document, a saved file, or a recording. Registration, a © symbol, and publication are not required. This is why a worksheet on a blog with no license statement is still protected, and why a teacher should treat it as all rights reserved unless the owner grants permission.

questions.question_text: Which list names the 5R permissions that an open license can grant?

options.A: Read, reuse, rewrite, resell, redistribute
options.B: Retain, reproduce, revise, resell, redistribute
options.C: Retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute
options.D: Reproduce, adapt, distribute, perform, display

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. David Wiley named the 5R permissions retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute. Option D is a tempting mix-up because it lists the five exclusive rights that copyright gives an owner: reproduce, adapt, distribute, perform, and display. Those are what an owner controls by default, while the 5Rs are what an open license hands to everyone else. Options A and B swap in words that are not part of the framework.

questions.question_text: What makes a material an educational resource?

options.A: Its format, because only textbooks, articles, and readings count as resources
options.B: Its price, because a resource must be free of charge to be used in teaching
options.C: Its purpose, because any material that supports teaching and learning counts, whatever its format
options.D: Its publisher, because the material must come from a school or a university

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. An educational resource is any material that a teacher or learner uses to support teaching and learning. The definition depends on purpose and not on format: a photograph of a canyon is a family snapshot in an album, and it becomes an educational resource when a teacher uses it to explain erosion. Texts, media, tools, assessments, and plans all qualify, so format (A), price (B), and publisher (D) do not decide it.

questions.question_text: Why is a publisher's free sample chapter marked "All rights reserved" not an OER?

options.A: It is only an excerpt, and OER must be complete books
options.B: It costs nothing but grants no permission to edit or share it
options.C: It comes from a company, and OER must come from universities
options.D: It is protected by copyright, and OER cannot be copyrighted by their creators

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. The sample chapter passes the price test but fails the permission test, because "All rights reserved" grants no permission to revise, remix, or redistribute it. OER can be a single worksheet, so length and source do not matter (A and C). OER are usually copyrighted too: an open license is a permission the owner grants on a protected work, so D reverses how openness works.

questions.question_text: Under the 5R framework, how does the revise permission differ from the remix permission?

options.A: Revise lets you share a work with others, while remix allows private use only
options.B: Revise applies to text only, while remix applies to images and video
options.C: Revise requires the author's approval each time, while remix does not
options.D: Revise changes a single work, while remix combines two or more works into something new

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Revising means adapting one work: fixing an error, translating it, or adding alt text. Remixing means joining the work with other open material, such as a unit built from chapters of two open textbooks. Echo's rule of thumb is to ask whether you changed one work or combined several. Sharing copies is the redistribute permission, so option A confuses two of the five. Neither permission is limited by media type or needs fresh approval.

questions.question_text: A teacher downloads an openly licensed textbook's PDF and its editable source files to her own laptop so that she still has them if the website goes offline. Which of the 5R permissions is she using?

options.A: Retain, because she is making and keeping her own copy
options.B: Reuse, because she is using the work in its original form
options.C: Revise, because the source files let her change the work
options.D: Redistribute, because she is moving copies between devices

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. The retain permission covers downloading, duplicating, storing, and managing your own copy. Websites change and disappear, and a bookmark is not a copy, so keeping the files protects next year's lesson. She has not yet changed the work (revise), taught with it (reuse), or given copies to others (redistribute). The test question for retain is, "Can I make and keep my own copy?"

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say that adopting an open textbook still requires evaluating it?

options.A: The license shows whether you may use the book, but not whether the book is good
options.B: Adopted resources must be revised before any student is allowed to read them
options.C: Open licenses expire unless the adopter checks the resource and renews the license each year
options.D: Adopting an open textbook transfers its copyright to the adopting teacher

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. The license answers "may I use it?", while the question "is it good?" stays open until someone checks. An open text may be out of date, may assume prior knowledge that your students lack, or may have no practice problems. Adoption means using the resource as it is, so revision is optional (B). Open licenses do not expire when unchecked (C), and adoption never transfers copyright (D). This gap is why the book teaches a rubric.

questions.question_text: In open pedagogy, how does a renewable assignment differ from a disposable assignment?

options.A: A renewable assignment is repeated every term by the same teacher, while a disposable one is given only once and never again
options.B: A renewable assignment is graded by classmates, while a disposable assignment is graded by the teacher alone
options.C: A renewable assignment uses a commercial textbook for its readings, while a disposable assignment uses an open textbook
options.D: A renewable assignment creates lasting value that others can reuse, while a disposable one is written, graded, and discarded

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. A disposable assignment is written, graded, and thrown away. A renewable assignment adds lasting value: for example, each anatomy student writes and illustrates one section of an open textbook that later cohorts revise. The word "renewable" refers to the work's lasting life, not to repeating the task (A) or to who grades it (B). Because students own their work, they must choose to release it openly.

questions.question_text: A department announces, "Our course is a zero textbook cost course because the library licenses the e-books, so it is built on OER." What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.A: Zero textbook cost describes price and OER describes permissions, so free library e-books can be zero cost without being open
options.B: Zero textbook cost courses may use only printed books and never e-books, because e-books always carry a fee
options.C: Library e-books are always in the public domain, so they need no license and no permission at all
options.D: OER must carry a price so that the open license can be funded, and a free course cannot be built on OER

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. A ZTC course means students pay nothing for required materials, and it often relies on OER, but it need not. Library-licensed e-books are free to read yet typically forbid copying, editing, and sharing, so they are free but not open. The department has confused the price dial with the permission dial. E-books are allowed in ZTC courses (B), library e-books are rarely public domain (C), and OER have no price requirement (D).

questions.question_text: What are the three layers that every Creative Commons license provides?

options.A: A plain-language summary, a court ruling, and a registration record
options.B: A Commons Deed, the legal code, and machine-readable code
options.C: A license name, a version number, and an author credit
options.D: A badge icon, a legal notice, and a copyright symbol

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Every CC license comes in three layers so that people, lawyers, and software can each read it. The Commons Deed is a short plain-language summary, the legal code is the full text a court would read, and the machine-readable code is metadata that lets search tools recognize the license. Options A, C, and D mix in items such as a court ruling, a version number, and a copyright symbol, which are not license layers.

questions.question_text: Which Creative Commons element requires that anyone who shares an adaptation must license it under the same license or a compatible one?

options.A: Attribution (BY)
options.B: ShareAlike (SA)
options.C: NonCommercial (NC)
options.D: NoDerivatives (ND)

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. ShareAlike (SA) keeps improvements open by requiring each adaptation to carry the same license, or one that the license lists as compatible. It applies only when you adapt the work, so sharing an unchanged copy needs only credit. Attribution (A) requires credit, NonCommercial (C) limits commercial use, and NoDerivatives (D) forbids sharing changed versions altogether. People call the ShareAlike approach copyleft.

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes an open license?

options.A: A license in which the owner gives one named person permission to use a work after that person asks
options.B: A license in which the owner keeps every right and allows the work to be viewed online
options.C: A license in which the owner gives everyone permission in advance, at no charge, to do things that copyright would otherwise reserve
options.D: A license in which the owner sells the right to change a work to anyone who pays a fee

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. An open license is public, in advance, and standing. The owner offers it to everyone and not to a named person, grants it before anyone asks, and people who received the work keep their rights even if the owner later stops offering it. It grants the five R permissions to the whole public, usually with conditions such as credit. Option A describes a one-time permission, and option B describes all rights reserved.

questions.question_text: What does TASL stand for in the credit-line format that Creative Commons recommends?

options.A: Title, Author, Source, License
options.B: Title, Attribution, Statement, License
options.C: Type, Author, Scope, Link
options.D: Title, Adaptation, Source, Link

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. TASL stands for Title, Author, Source, and License. Writing the four parts in order makes a credit line hard to get wrong: for example, "Watershed Basics" by Maria Lopez, a link to the work, licensed under CC BY 4.0. If you changed the work, add a sentence naming the change, such as "Adapted: reading level lowered." The other options mix in terms that are not part of the format.

questions.question_text: A teacher-sharing site marks a worksheet CC BY, but the worksheet's own pages say the uploader copied it from a publisher's book. What is the best conclusion?

options.A: The marking is worthless, because only an owner can grant a license and the uploader did not hold the rights
options.B: The marking is valid, because a license statement always overrides what the original source says
options.C: The marking is valid, because the license icon on the site proves the creator's intent
options.D: The marking is valid, but only after the uploader adds a version number and a link

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Only an owner can grant a license, and the uploader never held the rights to give away, so the marking carries no weight. This is why you trace a resource to its original creator and follow the license link back to the source. When a statement and its source disagree, the source wins. Icons and markings are easy to copy onto pages that never carried a license.

questions.question_text: Why can a CC BY-NC-SA work not be combined with a CC BY-SA work?

options.A: ShareAlike licenses may never be combined with any other Creative Commons license, whatever its elements
options.B: CC BY-NC-SA works are in the public domain, so they cannot be mixed with licensed works of any kind
options.C: Only works from the same creator can be combined under a ShareAlike license, so remixes need one author
options.D: One requires noncommercial use while the other keeps commercial use possible, so no single license satisfies both

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. CC BY-SA requires the combined work to be CC BY-SA, which allows commercial use, while CC BY-NC-SA requires the combined work to be CC BY-NC-SA, which does not. No single license meets both demands, so this is a license conflict. Option A is too broad, because a CC BY work combines with a CC BY-SA work. When you face a conflict, choose a different resource, ask an owner in writing, or keep the works separate.

questions.question_text: A teacher adds alt text to the images of a CC BY-ND chapter. What does the NoDerivatives requirement allow her to do with the changed copy?

options.A: She may not add alt text even to a private copy, because any change is forbidden
options.B: She may share the changed copy, but only if she keeps the use noncommercial
options.C: She may use the changed copy for her own reading, but she may not share it
options.D: She may share the changed copy as long as she credits the original author

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. NoDerivatives lets you share the work only as it is. It does not forbid private changes, so she may adjust a copy for her own study, but giving the changed copy to students or colleagues counts as sharing, and the license does not allow that. She can ask the owner for permission to share the improved version, or choose a resource that allows changes. Credit alone (D) does not lift the restriction.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes fair use in OER work?

options.A: It is a Creative Commons license that allows classroom copying of any work, with credit to the author
options.B: It guarantees that any educational use of a work is allowed without permission, whatever the amount copied
options.C: It lets you share a changed version of a whole textbook as long as you credit the author and keep the use educational
options.D: It is a case-by-case defense, not a license, and it does not cover sharing a changed copy of a whole resource

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Fair use is a U.S. legal doctrine that a court weighs case by case, usually after a dispute has begun, using four factors: purpose, nature of the work, amount used, and market effect. It is a defense, not a license, so you cannot know in advance how a court would rule. If a license already covers your use, rely on the license, and keep fair use in reserve for small excerpts.

questions.question_text: A teacher combines a chapter licensed CC BY with a chapter licensed CC BY-SA into one unit. Which license may the combined unit carry?

options.A: CC BY-SA, because the ShareAlike source requires it and CC BY accepts it
options.B: CC BY, because the more open license always governs the combined work
options.C: CC BY-NC, because mixing two licenses makes the combined work noncommercial
options.D: No license, because the two sources conflict and cannot be combined

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. The method is to write what each source requires of the combined work, then look for a license that satisfies every requirement. CC BY accepts any of the four licenses in the order CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, while CC BY-SA requires CC BY-SA, so CC BY-SA is the only license that meets both. This pair does not conflict. Option B reverses the logic, since the ShareAlike source sets the requirement.

questions.question_text: A teacher reviews three uses of a CC BY-NC worksheet: handing it out in a public-school class, posting it on a blog that earns paid advertising income, and using it in a $20 nonprofit workshop that charges to cover room and printing costs. Which reading matches the chapter's guidance?

options.A: All three are allowed, because none of the uses sells the worksheet itself for profit to a customer
options.B: Only the class handout is allowed, because charging any fee at all makes a use commercial and so forbidden
options.C: The class handout is allowed, the advertising blog is not, and the $20 workshop is unclear, so ask the owner
options.D: The class handout and the workshop are allowed, and the advertising blog is unclear because blogs are public

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Nobody earns money from the classroom handout, so it is allowed. Advertising income makes the blog's use commercial, so it is not allowed. Cost recovery is a gray area, so the workshop is unclear and the teacher should ask the owner in writing. NonCommercial is blurrier than it sounds, and the table in the chapter is a guide rather than legal advice. Option B treats every fee as commercial, which overstates the rule.

questions.question_text: How is the 100-point total of the ten-metric rubric divided?

options.A: Five quality metrics and five reusability metrics, each worth 10 points
options.B: Ten metrics with different weights, with accuracy worth the most points
options.C: Two dimensions, with quality worth 70 points and reusability worth 30 points
options.D: Seven quality metrics and three reusability metrics, each worth 10 points

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. The ten-metric rubric scores five quality metrics and five reusability metrics, each worth 10 points, so the quality subtotal and the reusability subtotal are each worth 50 points and the total is 100. Equal weights keep scores easy to compare between resources and reviewers. The numbers on the worksheet show the order of the rows, not the importance of the metrics.

questions.question_text: What three parts does good evidence for a score contain?

options.A: Where you looked, what you saw, and the rule you compared it with
options.B: Who reviewed it, when it was reviewed, and the final score
options.C: A quote, a screenshot, and a signature from a second reviewer
options.D: The metric name, the score, and the resource's total

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Evidence gives the location, such as a page, section, URL, or file; the observation, such as a quote, count, or measurement; and the rule, which is the check from the metric. With those three parts another reviewer can repeat your check and reach the same observation. Opinions such as "the facts seem right" and unchecked claims by an AI agent are not evidence yet.

questions.question_text: Which of these metrics belongs to the reusability dimension of the rubric?

options.A: Readability
options.B: Accessibility
options.C: Practice with feedback
options.D: Editable source

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. The five reusability metrics are open license, modularity, metadata, editable source, and portability. They measure how easily other people can find, change, and reuse a resource. Readability, accessibility, and practice with feedback belong to the quality dimension, along with accuracy and currency and alignment, because they measure how well the resource helps learners learn.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes an analytic rubric?

options.A: It gives one overall rating for the work, such as four stars
options.B: It scores several criteria separately and then combines the scores
options.C: It scores only the accuracy of the facts in a resource
options.D: It lets an AI agent choose the criteria for each review

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. An analytic rubric scores several criteria separately and then combines them. It takes longer than a holistic rubric, which gives a single overall rating, but it shows what to fix and lets different reviewers compare their scores. That is why this book uses an analytic rubric with ten metrics. A holistic rating such as four stars hides which part of a resource failed a learner.

questions.question_text: Three resources each total 65 points, yet the chapter says they call for three different actions. Why?

options.A: Totals are calculated by a different formula for each resource that is reviewed
options.B: The total hides the split between the two halves and the weakest metric
options.C: Each resource must be reviewed with a different rubric before its total can be used
options.D: A total of 65 is not a valid score on this rubric, so the resources must have been scored wrongly

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. The total is the sum of all ten metric scores, so it is the least informative number in a report. One resource may be weak on metadata, another locked by its license, and a third full of factual errors, yet all three total 65. Report the total together with the two subtotals and the lowest metric. Totals are most useful for comparing two versions of the same resource.

questions.question_text: What does it mean to say that a rubric is reliable but not valid?

options.A: It measures what matters, but different reviewers get quite different scores for the same resource
options.B: It produces scores only for resources that carry an open license and are written in English
options.C: It gives consistent scores, but the scores may not measure what matters to learners
options.D: It was written by experts, but no reviewer has ever used it to score a real resource

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Reliability is consistency: different reviewers, or the same reviewer later, produce similar scores. Validity is whether the scores measure what they claim to measure. A rubric can give the same wrong answer every time, like a scale that is steady but off. Option A describes the reverse case. Chapters 16 and 17 test validity by asking whether students learn more from resources that score higher.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter recommend that a reviewer finish all ten scores before looking at a colleague's or an AI agent's scores?

options.A: Scoring alone is faster because there are fewer metrics to check
options.B: Reviewers should never discuss their scores with anyone else
options.C: A colleague's score is likely to be wrong, while the reviewer's own is correct
options.D: A number seen first pulls judgment toward it, a bias called anchoring

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Anchoring means the first number you see or write pulls later judgments toward it, and you will not feel it happen. Scoring alone first, with evidence, protects each reviewer's independent judgment. Reviewers then compare metric by metric and discuss only the metrics where scores differ by more than 3 points. Discussion is part of the method, so option B is wrong, and neither score is assumed correct (C).

questions.question_text: Why does a reviewer start by writing down the resource's intended audience and learning outcomes?

options.A: The rubric awards 10 bonus points for each audience that a resource names in its description
options.B: Quality depends on the learner, so the resource is scored against what it was built to do
options.C: A resource without a stated audience cannot carry an open license, because licenses require an audience
options.D: The reviewer must prove that the intended audience likes the resource before any score is given

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. OER quality is the degree to which a resource helps its intended learners reach its intended outcomes, so it describes a relationship between a resource and a learner. A chemistry reading that is excellent for a first-year college class can be poor quality for a grade 8 class. A resource that states neither audience nor outcomes has a quality problem before the review begins.

questions.question_text: A reviewer scores a resource: accuracy 8, alignment 8, readability 9, accessibility 7, and practice 8, then open license 9, modularity 8, metadata 3, editable source 8, and portability 9. What do the chapter's total and adoption rule give?

options.A: Total 77, Adopt, because the total is at least 75 and so the rule is met
options.B: Total 77, Reject, because one metric scores below 5 and that always rules out a resource
options.C: Total 77, Revise, because one metric scores below the floor of 5
options.D: Total 74, Revise, because the total is below 75 and the metadata score is not counted

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. The quality scores add to 40 and the reusability scores add to 37, so the total is 77. That meets the total of 75, but metadata scores 3, which is below the floor of 5, so the Adopt rule is not met. The decision is Revise, because the total is at least 50. Reject applies only when the total is below 50. The floor stops one failed metric from hiding inside a high total.

questions.question_text: Two reviewers each total 65 for the same resource. Reviewer 1 scored accessibility 5 and portability 7, and Reviewer 2 scored accessibility 9 and portability 3. What does comparing the two worksheets show?

options.A: Two metrics are flagged because each differs by more than 3, so the matching totals hide real disagreement
options.B: The reviewers agree, because matching totals show that their scores are consistent on every metric
options.C: Neither metric is flagged, because the two differences cancel out in the total and so do not count
options.D: Only portability is flagged, because the reviewer who gave the lower score must justify that score

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. A metric agrees when the two scores differ by 3 points or fewer, and it is flagged when they differ by more than 3. Accessibility differs by 4 and portability differs by 4, so both are flagged even though the totals are identical. Compare reviewers metric by metric, then examine the evidence for each flagged metric. Reviewer 2 may have missed the video without captions, or Reviewer 1 may have missed a platform where the embed works.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: What is a fork of a repository?

options.A: A separate line of work inside the same repository that leaves the main line undisturbed
options.B: Your own independent copy of someone else's repository, which keeps a link back to the source
options.C: A proposal to merge changes from one copy of a repository into another copy, for the maintainer to review
options.D: A saved snapshot of changes, with an author, a date, and a message that says what was done

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. A fork is your own independent copy of someone else's repository, made on the same site. You can change it freely without affecting the original, and it keeps a link back to the source. Forking is the repository version of the revise and remix permissions: the open license gives you the right to change a resource, and the fork gives you the place to do it. Option A describes a branch, C a pull request, and D a commit.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: Which set of tests identifies an open file format?

options.A: The specification is published, anyone can implement it without paying, and free software opens it
options.B: The file is free to download, widely used, and created by a nonprofit organization
options.C: The file prints well, looks the same on every device, and is saved as a PDF by a design program
options.D: The file is plain text, is under one megabyte, and contains no images or any other media

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Three questions test a format: is the specification published, can anyone implement it without paying a fee or asking permission, and does free software exist that opens it? A format that passes all three stays readable when a company changes its products or closes. Price, popularity, printing quality, and file size say nothing about openness. A file can also be an open standard and still be a poor source for editing, as the PDF shows.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: Why is a resource that offers only a PDF a poor choice for a teacher who wants to revise it?

options.A: A PDF is a closed format that no free software can open, so it cannot be edited or even read at all
options.B: A PDF cannot carry an open license, so revision is not permitted even if the owner agrees
options.C: A PDF records how pages look, not how content is built, so a change means rebuilding the structure
options.D: A PDF is too large to download without creating a login, which blocks every revision attempt

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. A PDF is an open international standard and free software opens it, so option A is wrong. The problem is structure: a PDF records the appearance of each page, so changing a sentence means copying text out of the page, losing headings and tables, and rebuilding the layout. A license can be attached to a PDF, so the right to revise may exist even though the practical means do not. Ask the author for the source file.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: What is the difference between a source format and a delivery format?

options.A: A source format is always an open standard that free tools can read, while a delivery format is always a closed one
options.B: A source format is meant for readers who study the content, while a delivery format is meant for authors who write it
options.C: A source format keeps the structure so the content can be changed, while a delivery format is for reading or printing
options.D: A source format is stored on GitHub in a repository, while a delivery format is stored on a school website

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. The chapter compares a source to a recipe and a delivery file to a cake. You can change an ingredient in the recipe and bake again, but you cannot take the sugar out of the cake. A source format such as Markdown, HTML, or a word processing file keeps headings, lists, and links. A delivery format such as a PDF or a scan often keeps only the appearance. Where a file is stored (D) does not decide which kind it is.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: Why does version control help when several teachers improve the same open resource?

options.A: It stops anyone except the original author from changing the files, so no edits can conflict
options.B: It stores each person's edits in a separate copy that is never combined with the other copies
options.C: It converts every file to a PDF, so that all of the changes look the same to every reader
options.D: It records every change with an author, date, and message, combines edits, and can restore any earlier version

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Version control replaces a folder of confusing copies such as lesson_final2.docx with one set of files and a recorded history. A reviser can see exactly what changed, a mistake can be undone by returning to an earlier state, and several people can work at once and combine their changes. A reuser can also judge a resource's health from the date of its last change. Open resources depend on this, because anyone may revise them.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: A reviewer applies the ten editable source checks to a district unit. Check 3 (the source holds all of the content) and check 7 (a note explains how the pieces fit) fail, and the other eight pass. What score does the chapter's rule give?

options.A: 7, because 80 percent falls in the 7 to 8 band and the missing content blocks revision
options.B: 8, because 80 percent falls in the 7 to 8 band and the higher number is always used
options.C: 6, because each failed check lowers a score of 10 by two points
options.D: 5, because a failed check that blocks revision caps the score at 5

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Eight of ten checks pass, a share of 80 percent, which falls in the 7 to 8 band. Check 3 blocks revision when it fails, because a reviser cannot change content that is missing from the source. When a failed check blocks revision, choose the lower number in the band, so the score is 7. The higher number (B) is correct only when no failed check blocks revision, as with the image and change-record failures in the chapter's Watershed Basics example.

questions.question_text: Which line of Markdown shows an image whose alt text is "A river flowing through a valley"?

options.A: `[A river flowing through a valley](https://example.org/images/river.png)`
options.B: `![A river flowing through a valley](https://example.org/images/river.png)`
options.C: `![https://example.org/images/river.png](A river flowing through a valley)`
options.D: `## A river flowing through a valley`

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. An image uses the same pattern as a link, with an exclamation mark in front: square brackets hold the alt text, and parentheses hold the address. Option A has no exclamation mark, so it creates a link and not an image. Option C swaps the alt text and the address. Option D creates a level-2 heading. Alt text is the description that a screen reader speaks, so a reviser should never leave the brackets empty.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: A teacher finds a typo in an open lesson on GitHub and wants every teacher who uses the lesson to benefit from the fix. Which sequence should she follow?

options.A: Edit the original repository directly, then fork it to record the change
options.B: Fork the repository, fix the typo in her copy, then open a pull request to the original
options.C: Open a pull request first, then fork the repository and make the change
options.D: Fork the repository, fix the typo, and keep it in her fork, because pull requests are only for large changes

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. She forks the repository to make her own copy, makes the change in the fork, and then opens a pull request that proposes the change to the original. The maintainer reads it, comments, and may merge it. A pull request is how a small fix, such as a typo or missing alt text, travels to every teacher who uses the resource. A pull request needs a change to propose, so it cannot come first (C).

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: A reviewer opens a repository and finds a README, a LICENSE file stating CC BY 4.0, and Markdown source files. The latest commit is four years old, and several open issues report errors that nobody has answered. What does this evidence most strongly suggest?

options.A: The resource is high quality, because it uses open formats and an open license and has a README
options.B: The resource has no editable source, because its commits are old and the files are therefore locked
options.C: The license is invalid, because the repository is no longer active and the owner has not replied
options.D: The resource has an open license and editable source but may be unmaintained, so accuracy and currency need checking

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. The license file and Markdown files are good evidence for the open license and editable source metrics. A last commit that is years old suggests the resource is no longer maintained, and unanswered issues that report errors point to problems in accuracy and currency. Open formats say nothing about quality (A), and the age of the commits does not remove the source files (B) or invalidate the license (C). Evidence from a repository can be checked and cited.

questions.chapter: Open File Formats and Version Control
questions.question_text: A reviewer's editable source checks fail for four different resources. Which failed check would block a reviser from changing the content and so pull the score to the lower number in its band?

options.A: The images are PNG files, and no original or vector source files are offered for them
options.B: No short note explains how the pieces of the resource fit together or what each file does
options.C: The source file leaves out part of the content, such as tables and equations
options.D: No record of changes is available, such as a changelog or a list of past versions

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. A failed check blocks revision when a reviser cannot change the content without it. If the source omits tables or equations, those parts cannot be edited at all. A reviser can still change every word and replace any picture without the original image files (A), and a missing note (B) or change record (D) makes the work harder but does not stop it. The chapter marks checks 5, 7, and 8 as non-blocking.

questions.question_text: According to the chapter, when should a reviewer ask for an expert review?

options.A: When the resource shows a publication date and a revision history that are both recent
options.B: When the sampled facts all match, but the reviewer likes the writing style and the layout
options.C: When the claims bear on health, safety, or law, or the sample shows two or more mismatches in ten
options.D: When the resource carries an open license that allows commercial reuse and editing by anyone, anywhere

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Ask for an expert review when the topic is outside your knowledge, when the content bears on health, safety, or law, when claims are contested, or when your sample finds two or more mismatches in ten facts. A date, a revision history (A), and an open license (D) are useful evidence for other checks, and none of them calls for an expert. Liking the writing style (B) is an opinion, not evidence.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say to check each sampled fact against a source that is independent of the resource?

options.A: Independent sources are always free to read online, whereas the resource's references usually are not
options.B: Checking against another copy of the same text proves nothing, because copied errors spread
options.C: Only independent sources can be primary sources, and the resource's own references never can
options.D: An independent source is much easier to cite correctly than the resource's own list of references

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. If a reviewer compares a claim with a copy of the same text, a copied error will match and the check proves nothing. Choose a reliable source that was produced separately, such as an agency's current data page, and compare word for word and number for number. The sample should hold at least 10 checkable facts, spread across the sections, with numbers, dates, and names favored because they are likeliest to be wrong.

questions.question_text: Why must a reviewer record "not addressed" as its own fact-checking result instead of counting it as a match?

options.A: A source that does not mention a claim has shown that the claim is false and should be rejected
options.B: A source that never mentions a claim neither supports nor contradicts it, so silence cannot count as a match
options.C: Every claim that a source does not address must be removed from the resource by the reviewer
options.D: A source that is silent on one claim cannot be trusted for any other claim in the resource

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. A source can support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it. Silence is not support: a reviewer who counts it as a match will pass claims that no one actually checked. The reviewer should look for a source that does address the claim, or record the claim as not checkable and report it. Echo's reminder is that a source which never mentions a claim has not confirmed it.

questions.question_text: Which description matches a secondary source?

options.A: A review article that summarizes thirty studies done by other researchers
options.B: A lab notebook entry that records a measurement when it was made
options.C: A census table that gives the population count on the census date
options.D: A photograph taken at the library while the flood water was rising

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. A secondary source describes, summarizes, or interprets primary sources. Textbooks, review articles, news stories about research, and histories are secondary sources, and this book treats encyclopedias the same way. The other three options are primary sources, because each is original evidence from the time or person described. Secondary sources are useful but one step removed, so for an important claim a reviewer follows them back to a primary source.

questions.question_text: An AI-generated reference lists a real author, a working link, and a reputable publisher. Why might it still be a weak citation?

options.A: A working link means the page will disappear soon, which is called link rot by reviewers
options.B: A reputable publisher cannot be a reliable source for any claim, however well it is cited
options.C: A real author's work is always a secondary source and so cannot support a claim
options.D: The source may say nothing about the claim beside it, so it can fail the relevance test

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Citation quality asks four questions: is the source relevant, reliable, retrievable, and current? A real source with a working link can still say nothing about the claim, and AI agents are known to produce references that look right and are not. Open the source, read the line that supports the claim, and record that you did. Neither a working link (A) nor a reputable publisher (B) is a weakness.

questions.question_text: A reviewer applies the ten accuracy and currency checks to a clinic guide. Only check 2 fails, because fewer than 9 of every 10 sampled facts match, and the chapter marks that check as serious. What score does the scoring rule give?

options.A: 9, because 90 percent is in the 9 to 10 band and a serious failure selects the lower number
options.B: 10, because only one check in ten failed and so the higher number in the band is always used
options.C: 8, because a single serious failure always moves the score down one band
options.D: 5, because more than one in ten sampled facts did not match, which halves the score

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Nine of ten checks pass, a share of 90 percent, which falls in the 9 to 10 band. A failed check is serious when a learner could take away a false or outdated fact, and check 2 is serious, so the reviewer chooses the lower number, 9. A score of 10 requires every check to pass (B). A serious failure selects a number within the band and does not move the score to another band (C).

questions.question_text: A link checker reports a 301 result for a cited page, and the new address shows the same article. What should the reviewer do?

options.A: Keep the link unchanged, because the page still loads
options.B: Replace the source, because 301 means the page is gone for good
options.C: Update the link to the new address, because the page moved permanently
options.D: Open the link by hand later, because 301 means the server refused the tool

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. A 301 result means the page moved permanently to a new address, so the reviewer updates the link. A 404 calls for finding the new address or replacing the source, and a 410 means the page is gone for good, so replace it. A 403 means the server refused the tool, so open the link by hand. Record the date of the test, because a link that works today may fail next month.

questions.question_text: A reviewer reads four statements in a lab guide on 12 October 2026. Which statement shows the strongest sign of outdated content?

options.A: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen as plants make food
options.B: To sign in, click the blue Sign On button in the screenshot, which dates from 2015
options.C: The United States Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776 by the Continental Congress
options.D: The area of a rectangle is its length times its width, measured in square units

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Content ages at different speeds, so a reviewer matches the checking to how fast the topic moves. Software screenshots, prices, and web addresses age quickly, and an interface screenshot from 2015 is likely to have been redesigned. Basic science, mathematics, and historical dates change very slowly or not at all. Outdated content was correct when written, which is why the author did nothing wrong at the time and a learner is harmed all the same.

questions.question_text: A resource states "Wetlands filter pollutants" and cites a textbook. The textbook cites a review article, and the review summarizes several studies. A reviewer stops after confirming that the textbook says the same thing. What has the reviewer actually shown?

options.A: That the claim is fully supported by primary evidence at the end of the citation chain
options.B: That the claim is false, because textbooks are never reliable sources for a scientific claim
options.C: That the citation chain is broken at the textbook and cannot be followed any further back
options.D: That a secondary source agrees with the resource, not that the original evidence supports the claim

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Citations form chains, and an error can enter at any link. The textbook is a secondary source, and the review is another step removed. A reviewer who stops at the textbook has found only that a textbook agreed with the resource. Following the chain to the study that reported the measurements before and after water passed through a wetland gives a check that can be trusted. The further back you trace a claim, the stronger the check.

questions.question_text: Resource A was carefully written in 2012 and had no errors on the day it was published, but it has never been updated. Resource B was published last month and gives a wrong date for a historical event. Which analysis is correct?

options.A: Both fail on accuracy, because neither resource's facts can be trusted by a careful reader today
options.B: Resource A fails on accuracy, because it is old, and Resource B fails on currency
options.C: Resource A passes both halves, because it contained no errors when it was published
options.D: Resource A is weak on currency though accurate when written, and Resource B fails on accuracy

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Accuracy asks whether the facts were correct when written, and currency asks whether they are still correct now. A careful 2012 text can score well on one half and badly on the other, because facts, figures, software, and links age. Resource A is a currency problem. Resource B contains a false statement from the start, so it is an accuracy problem. The two halves together make up the first quality metric.

questions.question_text: Which verb is measurable, meaning a teacher could observe a learner doing it?

options.A: Understand
options.B: Calculate
options.C: Appreciate
options.D: Be familiar with

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. A measurable verb names something a teacher could watch a learner do and check afterward. List, describe, calculate, compare, and design are measurable. Know, understand, learn, appreciate, and be familiar with are not, because no one can see them happen. A quick test is to ask, "How would I know the learner did this?" If the answer is "I couldn't tell," swap in a verb such as explain or label.

questions.question_text: Which three parts make up a well-formed learning objective in the model the chapter uses?

options.A: Topic, activity, and assessment
options.B: Outcome, standard, and sequence
options.C: Audience, verb, and grade level
options.D: Performance, condition, and criterion

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. The model comes from the educator Robert Mager. The performance is what the learner will do, written with a measurable verb. The condition is the situation or help the learner has, such as "given a map." The criterion is how well the learner must do it, such as "with no more than one error." An objective written this way can be assessed, unlike "Students will learn about runoff."

questions.question_text: Which list shows the six levels of the revised Bloom's taxonomy in order from the simplest to the most demanding?

options.A: Remember, understand, apply, evaluate, analyze, create
options.B: Understand, remember, apply, analyze, evaluate, create
options.C: Remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create
options.D: Remember, apply, understand, analyze, create, evaluate

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. The 2001 revision by Anderson and Krathwohl orders the levels remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create, and each level asks more of the learner than the one before. The order matters to a reviewer because an outcome and the activities that teach it should sit at the same level. If an outcome says "predict" and every activity asks only for recall, learners never practice the skill the outcome names.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say that a standard code printed beside an activity is not evidence of alignment?

options.A: The code states what the author hopes, so a reviewer must read the standard and check what learners do
options.B: Standard codes are usually out of date by the time a resource is published and reviewed
options.C: Only state standards can be matched to activities, and codes come from national bodies
options.D: A code shows that the activity matches the standard, but at the Remember level only

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Listing a code is not matching. The reviewer reads the standard, finds the verb it asks for, and looks for an activity that asks learners to do that. A strong match has learners doing what the standard names, a partial match touches the topic without the performance, and no match shares only a topic word. For example, coloring a picture of a river does not meet a standard that asks learners to explain how water moves.

questions.question_text: An outcome says "Explain how water moves over land," but every quiz item asks learners to choose a vocabulary word. What is the problem?

options.A: The outcome uses a vague verb such as 'know', so no quiz item could check it
options.B: The items check a different topic from the one that the outcome names
options.C: The items check the right topic at a lower level than the outcome asks
options.D: The outcome has no activity, so nothing in the resource teaches it to learners

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. An assessment item is aligned when it checks the outcome at the level the outcome asks. Here the topic matches, but "explain" asks for understanding and the items ask only for recall, so the level is wrong. This failure is easy to miss because the topic lines up. The fix is to raise the level of the questions. "Explain" is a measurable verb (A), and the problem lies in the items, not the teaching (D).

questions.question_text: Why can a passage score as easy on the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level and still be hard to read?

options.A: The formula works only on passages of more than 1,000 words, and short samples give no result
options.B: The formula measures vocabulary tiers and ignores sentence length, so it misses long sentences
options.C: The formula gives a score out of 10 and not a school grade, so it cannot show reading level
options.D: The formula counts sentence and word length, so it cannot see dense ideas, undefined terms, or poor organization

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. The formula uses three counts: sentences, words, and syllables. It measures the surface of the text. A passage of short words and short sentences can score as easy and still be hard if its ideas are dense or its terms are never defined. Treat the number as one piece of evidence and read the passage yourself. For a stable result, use passages of at least 100 words, not 1,000.

questions.question_text: A passage has 5 sentences, 100 words, and 150 syllables. Using grade = 0.39 × (words ÷ sentences) + 11.8 × (syllables ÷ words) − 15.59, what is its Flesch-Kincaid grade level?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Words per sentence is 100 divided by 5, which is 20, and 0.39 times 20 is 7.8. Syllables per word is 150 divided by 100, which is 1.5, and 11.8 times 1.5 is 17.7. Adding gives 25.5, and subtracting 15.59 gives 9.91, which rounds to 9.9. Option A stops after the sentence part, and option D forgets the final subtraction that lines the result up with school grades.

questions.question_text: Which rewrite of "Utilize the glossary for the purpose of locating unfamiliar terms" is plainest while keeping the meaning?

options.A: Look at the glossary
options.B: Utilize the glossary to locate terms
options.C: Use of the glossary is advised for the location of unfamiliar terms
options.D: Use the glossary to find words you do not know

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Plain language uses short sentences with one idea, the active voice, and common words where a common word is as accurate. Option D keeps both the action and the purpose in everyday words. Option A is short but loses the purpose, option B keeps the stiff word "utilize," and option C buries the action in a passive, noun-heavy phrase. Plain language is not dumbing down, because the ideas stay the same and the clutter goes away.

questions.question_text: A water unit has four sections. Section 1 introduces watershed and tributary. Section 2 introduces runoff and uses watershed. Section 3 introduces flood and uses runoff and infiltration. Section 4 introduces infiltration and uses runoff. What is the sequence problem, and how is it fixed?

options.A: Section 3 uses infiltration before section 4 introduces it, so section 4 should move up before section 3
options.B: Section 2 uses watershed before it is introduced, so section 2 should come before section 1
options.C: Section 4 uses runoff before it is introduced, so section 4 should come before section 2
options.D: There is no problem, because every idea is introduced somewhere in the unit before the quiz

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. To check sequence, list what each section introduces and what it uses, then look for a section that uses an idea that arrives later. Section 3 uses infiltration, but section 4 is where infiltration is introduced, so learners meet the idea before they are taught it. Moving section 4 ahead of section 3 fixes it. Option D is the misconception that an idea appearing anywhere in the unit is enough.

questions.question_text: In a curriculum map for a fraction unit, the outcome "Add two fractions with the same denominator" is taught by Section 3, but no quiz item checks it. How should a reviewer classify and fix this?

options.A: A content gap in teaching, so add a new section that teaches the outcome to learners
options.B: Content with no outcome, so delete Section 3 from the unit to shorten the resource
options.C: A content gap in checking, so add a quiz item that checks the outcome at the level it asks
options.D: A level mismatch in teaching, so raise the Bloom level of Section 3

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. A content gap is an outcome that is not taught, not assessed, or not assessed at the level it asks. The gap can lie in the teaching, in the checking, or in both, and the fix differs: add an activity, add a question, or raise the level of the question. Here the outcome is taught but never checked, so the fix is a quiz item. The reverse problem, content with no outcome, is noted but is not a gap.

questions.question_text: What are the four principles of WCAG, often abbreviated POUR?

options.A: Perceivable, organized, usable, and reliable
options.B: Photographic, operable, universal, and readable
options.C: Practical, open, understandable, and responsive across devices
options.D: Perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines group their testable success criteria under four principles. Content must be perceivable, so users can sense it through sight or hearing or touch. It must be operable, including without a mouse. It must be understandable, so users can follow what it says and how it works. And it must be robust, so it works with browsers and assistive technology. Each criterion carries a level of A, AA, or AAA.

questions.question_text: What does conformance to WCAG 2.1 AA require?

options.A: Meeting every level A criterion and every level AA criterion
options.B: Meeting only the level AA criteria and none of the level A criteria
options.C: Meeting every level A, level AA, and level AAA criterion
options.D: Passing an automated accessibility checker with no errors

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. WCAG 2.1 AA is version 2.1 at conformance level AA, which means a resource meets every level A criterion and every level AA criterion. This book targets it because many school and college policies cite it, and because it protects the main groups of learners while staying practical for a teacher to check. Level AAA is the highest level and is not required for whole sites, and a clean checker report (D) is not the same as conformance.

questions.question_text: How should a decorative image, such as a thin border line, be marked in HTML so that a screen reader skips it?

options.A: Leave out the alt attribute entirely so that the reader skips the image altogether
options.B: Give it alt text that says "decoration" so that readers know it is not content
options.C: Use its file name as the alt text so that the image is still identified
options.D: Give it an empty alt attribute, written as `alt=""`, so that the reader skips it

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. A decorative image adds appearance only, so a screen reader should skip it, and an empty alt attribute tells the reader to do that. An image with no alt attribute at all is a different case, because many screen readers then read out the file name, which is useless. Alt text that says "decoration" (B) makes the reader announce something that carries no information. When a learner might wonder what the image is, write a short description instead.

questions.question_text: Why should alt text describe what an image does in its context instead of only how it looks?

options.A: Screen readers cannot announce descriptions that are longer than one word, so short text is always required
options.B: A reader who cannot see the image needs text that does the same job the image does for a sighted reader
options.C: Alt text is shown only on printed copies of a page, where the appearance of an image does not matter
options.D: Describing the appearance would repeat the page's heading and so add nothing for the reader

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Good alt text answers "what does this image do here?" A photo of a river in a lesson about meanders needs alt text that mentions the bends, while the same photo used only for mood needs none. Say what matters in a sentence or two, do not begin with "image of," do not repeat an adjacent caption, and never leave a file name or a single word such as "photo."

questions.question_text: Which media alternative narrates the important visual information in a video that the soundtrack does not already give?

options.A: Captions
options.B: Keyboard navigation
options.C: Color independence
options.D: Audio description

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Audio description is spoken narration of actions, scene changes, on-screen text, and charts. It serves learners who are blind or have low vision, and it fills the gap when an instructor says "as you can see here" and points to a chart that is never described. Captions (A) are timed text of speech and important sounds for learners who cannot hear. At level AA, prerecorded video with sound needs captions and audio description.

questions.question_text: A page contains an image with no alt attribute, and the image file is named river.png. What does a screen reader typically say?

options.A: "Image, river dot png," reading the file name aloud to the listener
options.B: Nothing, because the image is skipped and the reader moves on to the next element
options.C: "Image, a river," describing the picture to the listener in words
options.D: "Image, decorative," announcing that the image carries no meaning

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. A screen reader reads the page's underlying structure and does not look at the picture, so without alt text it often falls back on the file name. That is useless to the listener. An empty alt attribute is what makes a reader skip an image (B), and no screen reader describes a photo by itself (C). Wording varies between programs, so listen to a page for five minutes before you score.

questions.question_text: A reviewer measures four text-and-background pairs. Which one passes for normal-size body text under WCAG 2.1 AA?

options.A: Gray on white with a contrast ratio of 4.61 to 1
options.B: Gray on white with a contrast ratio of 3.03 to 1
options.C: White on orange with a contrast ratio of 2.33 to 1
options.D: Pale gray on white with a contrast ratio of 1.36 to 1

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1. A ratio of 3.03 to 1 (B) meets only the 3 to 1 minimum for large text, which means at least 18 points, or 14 points if bold. The other two pairs fail for every size. Pass or fail can hinge on a difference no one can see, so reviewers measure with a tool instead of judging by eye.

questions.question_text: A reviewer applies the ten accessibility checks to a lecture video series. Check 7 (captions), check 8 (transcripts or audio description), and check 10 (page language, link text, table headers) fail, and the other seven pass. What score does the chapter's rule give?

options.A: 6, because 70 percent falls in the 5 to 6 band and the higher number applies
options.B: 7, because seven checks passed, so the score equals the number of passes
options.C: 5, because 70 percent falls in the 5 to 6 band and uncaptioned video is a serious failure
options.D: 3, because three checks failed, so the score equals the number of failures

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Seven of ten checks pass, a share of 70 percent, which falls in the 5 to 6 band. A failed check is serious when it keeps a group of learners out of the content altogether, and video with no captions is one of the named examples. When a serious check fails, choose the lower number in the band, so the score is 5. The higher number (A) applies only when no serious check fails.

questions.question_text: An automated checker reports zero errors for a page, but every image on the page has the alt text "photo." Which analysis is correct?

options.A: The page passes the accessibility metric, because the tool reports no errors on any of its images
options.B: The checker is faulty, because any good checker would flag one-word alt text as a failure
options.C: The checker confirms alt text exists but cannot judge whether it is useful, so the page still fails that check
options.D: Alt text is no longer required once an automated checker reports no errors for the page

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. A checker finds real problems quickly, such as images with no alt attribute, weak contrast, and unlabeled form fields. It cannot tell whether alt text is useful, and it cannot tell whether a heading describes its section. A clean report is therefore not a pass. Run the tool, then do the human checks: read the alt text, listen with a screen reader, and tab through the page.

questions.question_text: A chart marks the winning team in green and the losing team in red and offers no other cue. Which learners does this exclude, and what is the fix?

options.A: Only learners who use a screen reader, so add alt text to the chart and nothing else
options.B: Learners who are color blind or print in gray, so add a second cue such as a label, pattern, or icon
options.C: Only learners who are deaf or hard of hearing, so add captions to the chart
options.D: No one, because red and green contrast strongly, so no change is needed to the chart

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Color independence means color is never the only way a resource conveys information. A learner who is color blind cannot tell the two colors apart, and a learner who prints in gray loses the distinction. Strong contrast between two colors does not help when the difference is in hue (D). The same rule applies to links in a paragraph, which need an underline or another cue beyond a slightly different color.

questions.question_text: What are the three parts of a multiple-choice question?

options.A: The stem, the key, and the distractors
options.B: The prompt, the rubric, and the answer key
options.C: The stem, the feedback message, and the question bank
options.D: The key, the outcome tag, and the retry control

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. The stem is the question or incomplete statement, the key is the correct option, and the distractors are the wrong options. Multiple-choice questions are easy for a computer to score and fast to answer, but they test recognition more easily than the ability to produce an answer, so a good quiz includes other kinds too. A feedback message, a tag, and a retry control are useful extras and not parts of the question itself.

questions.question_text: Which term names practice in which the learner tries to recall something from memory without looking at the source?

options.A: Spaced practice
options.B: Massed practice
options.C: Retrieval practice
options.D: Summative assessment

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Retrieval practice includes answering a question, writing down what you remember of a chapter, and using flash cards. Research on the testing effect finds that retrieving information strengthens memory more than rereading it, and it works best when feedback follows. Spaced practice (A) and massed practice (B) describe when practice happens, not what the learner does, so a plan can be retrieval and spaced at once.

questions.question_text: How does a worked solution differ from a worked example?

options.A: A worked example gives only final answers, while a worked solution gives every step of the method
options.B: A worked example comes before the learner tries, as a model, while a worked solution comes after an attempt
options.C: A worked example is written for teachers, while a worked solution is written for learners
options.D: A worked example appears after the attempt, while a worked solution appears before it

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Both show a full step-by-step solution, and the difference is timing and purpose. A worked example comes before practice as a model of the method. A worked solution comes after the learner's attempt, so the learner can find where their own method went wrong. An answer key, by contrast, shows only the final answers (A). Option D reverses the order.

questions.question_text: Which pair correctly contrasts formative and summative assessment?

options.A: Formative assessment is always graded, while summative assessment is never graded at all
options.B: Formative assessment comes at the end of a unit, while summative assessment happens during learning
options.C: Formative assessment guides learning as it happens, while summative assessment judges what was learned at the end
options.D: Formative assessment uses only multiple-choice items, while summative assessment uses only essays

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Formative assessment is assessment for learning: it is low stakes, often ungraded, repeatable, and used to adjust what comes next. Summative assessment, such as a final exam or a certificate exam, judges what was learned at the end. The same format can serve either purpose, so the question to ask is what the result is used for. A quiz in an open resource is usually a formative tool.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say that a quiz ending with "You got 5 of 8" has not given the learner useful feedback?

options.A: A score always arrives too late to affect what the learner does next, however soon it is shown to them
options.B: Quizzes should never show scores to learners, because scores discourage them from trying again
options.C: Feedback must always be delivered in person by a teacher, because software cannot explain
options.D: A score says how the learner did but not why, so nothing explains or corrects a misunderstanding

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. A feedback message is the part of practice that does the teaching. A strong message confirms or corrects the answer, says why, and, when the answer was wrong, names the likely misunderstanding and points to what to review. A total can hide that explanations are missing, so a reviewer opens each item and looks for a message. Online resources can show this feedback immediately and automatically, which print cannot match.

questions.question_text: Why do worked examples often help learners who are new to a topic more than solving the same problems unaided?

options.A: Beginners learn more from guessing before they see any solution, because errors are memorable
options.B: Solving from scratch uses attention that a beginner needs to see the method, so studying a full solution helps
options.C: Worked examples remove the need for any practice problems, because the method is already shown
options.D: Worked examples let learners skip feedback because the steps are already shown to them

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. Research on the worked example effect, associated with John Sweller and colleagues, finds that novices often learn more from studying worked examples because problem solving from scratch takes the attention they need to see the method. The best examples show each step and the reason for it. As skill grows, examples can fade, leaving steps for the learner to fill in. Practice problems are still needed, because a worked example never lets the learner try the method.

questions.question_text: A learner answers "Which describes infiltration?" with "Water flowing over the ground." Which feedback message best follows the chapter's guidance?

options.A: "Not quite. That is runoff, which flows over the ground. Infiltration is water soaking in, so review the two."
options.B: "Wrong. Try again, and this time read the question and all four options more carefully before you answer."
options.C: "Incorrect. The answer is the first option, so mark it as correct and move on to the next question when you are ready."
options.D: "Good try! Keep going, because you are doing well and the next question is easier than this one was."

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. A strong message corrects the answer, explains why, names the likely mix-up, and points to what to review, without blaming the learner. Option A says that the chosen answer describes runoff and defines infiltration as its opposite. "Wrong" (B) and the bare answer (C) say what failed or what is right without a reason. "Good try" (D) does not even say whether the answer was correct, which makes it unhelpful.

questions.question_text: A student closes the book and quizzes themself with flash cards on Monday, again on Thursday, and again the following Monday. How should this plan be classified?

options.A: Retrieval practice, spaced across several days
options.B: Rereading, spaced over several days with gaps between the sessions
options.C: Retrieval practice, massed into one long sitting
options.D: Rereading, massed into one sitting the night before

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **A**. Quizzing with the book closed is retrieval practice, because the learner tries to recall without looking. The gaps of several days between sessions make the practice spaced, and the spacing effect is among the most reliable findings in the study of learning. Retrieval and spacing are independent ideas: a plan can have one without the other. Cramming flash cards for three hours the evening before an exam would be retrieval that is massed (C).

questions.question_text: A reviewer reads this question: "Which caused increased runoff? A. Paving. B. Bare soil. C. Heavy rain. D. All of the above." What is the main flaw?

options.A: The stem is written in the negative, which makes learners reverse their thinking before answering
options.B: The key is noticeably longer than the other options, which gives the answer away
options.C: A grammatical clue before the options points to the key, so learners can guess it
options.D: "All of the above" lets a learner who knows two options are right guess the third without testing it

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. The chapter lists seven common flaws in multiple-choice questions: an ambiguous stem, an implausible distractor, a longer key, an "all of the above" option, a negative stem, a grammatical clue, and a pattern in key positions. This question has none of the others. Each option is short, the stem is positive, and no article points to an answer. A learner who recognizes two correct options can guess the third without knowing anything about it.

questions.question_text: A reviewer finds that a unit has no practice questions at all, only one worked example. How does the chapter's scoring rule treat the other practice checks, and what is the effect on the score?

options.A: Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as passed because they do not apply, so the score stays high
options.B: Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 are skipped, and only check 7, the worked example, is scored
options.C: Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as failed because check 1 fails, and the serious failure selects the lower number
options.D: Checks 2 to 5, 9, and 10 count as failed, but the higher number applies because the worked example passes

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Check 1 asks whether the resource offers practice with feedback on at least some items, and it is the one serious check. When it fails, the checks that depend on practice existing, which are 2 to 5, 9, and 10, count as failed. In the chapter's Reading Only Unit only the worked example passes, a share of 10 percent, and the serious failure selects the lower number, so the score is 1. Practice with no feedback, or feedback with no practice, is not enough.

questions.question_text: What does a reviewer do in the lift test for a standalone component?

options.A: Counts how many pages the component spans in the original resource and compares it with the other components
options.B: Copies the component to a new place and checks that it still works there with everything it needs
options.C: Asks the author whether the component was intended to stand alone, and accepts the answer
options.D: Runs an automated accessibility checker on the component and records the number of errors

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **B**. A standalone component works on its own, without the rest of the resource around it. The test is to lift it out: copy the piece into an empty file and read it cold. A reading that begins "as we saw in the last section" fails, a quiz that refers to "the diagram above" fails, and a simulation that needs a script from a sibling folder fails. A component passes when everything it needs travels with it.

questions.question_text: In Dublin Core, which element holds a resource's license or rights statement?

options.A: Source
options.B: Relation
options.C: Description
options.D: Rights

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **D**. Dublin Core is a standard vocabulary of 15 core elements. The Rights element records the license or rights statement, which is why this book's license field maps to it. Author maps to Creator, and grade level uses the education level term because Dublin Core has no core element for it. Source (A) records a resource from which this one is derived, and Relation (B) records a related resource.

questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say that a wrong value in a metadata field is worse than a blank field?

options.A: Blank fields are scored as valid, while wrong values are scored as invalid
options.B: A blank field lets a search tool fill in the correct value automatically
options.C: A wrong value makes a record look complete and sends searchers to the wrong place
options.D: A wrong value always makes the resource fail the open license metric

questions.explanation: The correct answer is **C**. Metadata completeness counts fields filled with valid values. A placeholder such as "TBD", a guess, or a license that does not match the page counts as invalid, so the record looks complete when it is not. It also misleads: a record that says CC BY next to a page that says CC BY-NC invites a dispute. Leave a field empty until you know the value, and then count it as missing.

questions.question_text: How do subject terms differ from keywords in a metadata record?

options.A: Subject terms are written for machines to read, while keywords are written only for people
